The Common Merganser (Mergus merganser) is a large, piscivorous diving duck with a life history well-adapted to northern freshwater ecosystems. Field data indicate that during incubation, a key developmental temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] is maintained within the nest, and under these conditions the eggs hatch after an incubation period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. This incubation duration is similar to that of other large sawbills and reflects the energetic demands of producing precocial young. Upon hatching, the downy chicks emerge with a relatively substantial wet weight at birth of 41.5 grams [Wwb = 41.5 grams], a mass that provides them with sufficient energy reserves for immediate mobility and early foraging. The brood is led to water shortly after hatching, where the young begin feeding on aquatic invertebrates under the watchful guidance of the female, a strategy that trades predator exposure for rapid access to prey.

Reproductive output in this species is best described through its clutch size and nesting frequency. Females typically lay a single clutch containing about 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = about 10 eggs per clutch] each breeding season, and field studies confirm that most successfully breeding adults produce just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. When the thermal conditions associated with active adult metabolism are considered, approximately 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], this annual rhythm of a single large clutch defines a relatively low maximum reproductive rate for a bird of this body size. The trade-off between egg size and number is evident, as the substantial mass of each neonate contributes to the chicks' cold tolerance and rapid swimming ability, enabling them to exploit productive but thermally challenging northern waters immediately after leaving the nest.

The developmental trajectory from hatching to independence is tightly constrained by the need to acquire flight feathers and foraging proficiency before the onset of winter. At the typical adult body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], which reflects the high metabolic demands of active diving and flight, the time since birth at fledging is documented at 74 days [tx = 74 days]. This period is characterized by rapid wing growth and the transition from a diet of aquatic insects to one dominated by fish, a shift that is gradual but essential for over-winter survival. Following fledging, the young birds undergo a period of refinement in their diving and pursuit skills, remaining dependent on the female for protection but increasingly responsible for their own prey capture. The duration of this post-fledging dependency is relatively short compared to some other waterfowl, allowing the young to disperse before lakes begin to freeze.

The onset of reproductive capability occurs considerably later than fledging, reflecting the time required for young mergansers to reach full adult size and secure suitable breeding territories. At the same metabolic body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the estimated time elapsed since birth at puberty is 222 days [tp = 222 days]. This marker indicates that while birds are physiologically capable of breeding in their first spring, competition for nest cavities and the advantages of experience often defer actual first breeding. The ultimate adult mass, recorded at 1445 grams [Wwi = 1445 grams], is achieved by the end of the first winter and represents a nearly 35-fold increase from the hatching mass, a growth trajectory that demands sustained access to abundant fish prey. This substantial body size confers an advantage in thermoregulation and competitive interactions over smaller duck species.

Longevity records and the timing of first successful reproduction further define the species' life history strategy. In the wild, the maximum documented lifespan is approximately 14.8 years [am = approximately 14.8 years] at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], reflecting a relatively slow pace of life for a bird of its trophic level.
